justice: A very wide paved roadway occupies most of the visible space, while no clearly designated sidewalk or pedestrian zone is visible, suggesting spatial resources are distributed more toward vehicle movement than toward all users equally.

The roadside green strip with trees and hedge provides environmental value, but it is not designed as an accessible public walking space because there is no visible curb ramp, crossing point, or marked pedestrian path.

Accessibility appears limited because the image shows a continuous paved edge and grass verge but no tactile paving, no detectable pedestrian guidance, and no barrier-free crossing facilities visible for users with different mobility needs.
safety: The road surface is wide, flat, and well maintained, which likely supports stable vehicle operation and reduces immediate surface hazards.
No marked pedestrian crossing, refuge island, or traffic calming feature is visible, so people on foot would have limited protected space if they needed to move along or across this corridor.
The roadside vegetation line separates the road from the deeper landscape, but there is no visible dedicated sidewalk or bike lane to reduce conflicts among different road users.
livability: The scene appears quiet and low density, with substantial greenery from trees, hedge, and grass, which can improve environmental quality.
However, there are no visible benches, shops, bus stops, building entrances, or social activity nodes, so the street offers little support for daily public life beyond movement.
The edge condition is dominated by hedge and planting rather than active frontage, making the space feel more like a transport edge than a lively, multifunctional street.
sustainability: The continuous row of trees, hedge planting, and grass verge contributes visible green infrastructure and some ecological value.
Street trees can provide shade and carbon benefits over time, although canopy coverage is still moderate and does not yet strongly cool the paved area.

No dedicated transit stop, bike lane, or obvious stormwater feature such as a bioswale is visible, so sustainability support is present mainly through landscaping rather than multimodal infrastructure.
aesthetics: The roadside planting is visually coherent, with evenly spaced trees and a continuous hedge creating an orderly green edge.
The pavement appears clean and well maintained, which improves the overall visual quality of the streetscape.
The open sky, simple composition, and consistent vegetation give the scene a calm and uncluttered appearance, though it is somewhat monotonous due to the lack of architectural or human-scale detail.
comfort: The road surface looks smooth and even, which supports physical comfort for travel on wheels and reduces vibration compared with rougher paving.
Trees are present along the verge, but their canopies are relatively small and cast limited shade onto the paved area, so thermal comfort is only moderate in sunny conditions.
The scene appears uncrowded and quiet, with no visible congestion or dense activity, which likely supports psychological comfort, but there are no seats or sheltered resting places.
walkability: Walkability is constrained because no clearly separated sidewalk is visible alongside the wide paved carriageway.
There are no visible crosswalk markings, curb ramps, or pedestrian signals, so route continuity and crossing convenience for walkers cannot be confirmed.
Although the green verge and trees make the edge more pleasant visually, the lack of dedicated pedestrian infrastructure means the corridor appears only weakly supportive of walking.
